title: Tzav: seven days at the door (Leviticus 8:33–35)
hook: the priests wait seven days at the entrance before serving

segments.voice: Yesterday, in Tzav, the priests marked on ear, thumb and toe. Your line was listen, do, walk. Who did you listen to fully? Day three hundred eighty-nine.

The robes are on. The oil has been poured on Aaron's head. The blood is on ear, thumb and toe. Everything is ready. If this were a movie, the next scene would be Aaron striding into the sanctuary to begin his life's work. Instead, Moses gives the new priests an instruction that sounds almost like a letdown. Don't go anywhere. Stay right here, at the entrance of the tent, day and night. Not for an hour. For a week. The work they've been dressed for will have to wait.
screen: `ROBES ON, OIL POURED.` → `READY TO BEGIN.` → `INSTEAD: STAY AT THE ENTRANCE.`

segments.voice: The verses say: you shall not go out from the entrance of the tent of meeting for seven days, until the days of your ordination are complete. Stay at the entrance day and night for seven days, and keep the charge of the Lord. The Hebrew for these days of ordination is milu'im, from a root meaning filling. In biblical Hebrew, to ordain a priest is literally to fill his hands. So these seven days are filling days. Not days of doing. Days of being filled. What were they doing at the door all week? The text doesn't say much. Offerings were repeated each day, and the priests ate their portion at the entrance. Mostly, they waited, in the doorway between the camp and the holy place. Neither outside nor fully in. And seven days is not a random number. It's the length of creation, the week every Jew lives by. The rabbis took this week seriously enough to build on it. The Talmud, at the start of the tractate on Yom Kippur, learns from these verses that the high priest should be set apart for seven days before the holiest day of the year, to prepare. The Mishnah sets apart the priest who burned the red heifer for seven days as well. In this part of the Torah, the holiest work doesn't start the moment someone is ready. It starts after a week of standing in the doorway, hands being filled.
screen: `DON'T LEAVE THE ENTRANCE.` · `MILU'IM: FILLING THE HANDS.` · `A WEEK IN THE DOORWAY.` · `SEVEN DAYS BEFORE YOM KIPPUR.` · then, large: `WAIT AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wait at the door. Settle, and breathe. Think of something big you're about to start, or want to: a move, a project, a hard conversation, a new habit. Instead of planning it, just stand at its entrance for a minute. Picture the doorway. Don't step through yet. Notice what you hope for. Notice what you're afraid of. Rest your hands open in your lap, empty, the way the priests' hands were before they were filled. The bell holds the time.
Tzav. Command. The portion that ends with the new priests waiting seven days at the entrance of the tent, before they serve.
Your line: wait at the door. Before you start something big this week, give it one deliberate pause at the threshold. Day three hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Following the Talmud's reading of these verses, the high priest in the Second Temple was set apart for seven days before Yom Kippur to prepare for the day's service.

original.note: Hebrew: filling, the name for the days of ordination.

trapdoor: what you thought: a waiting period before the priests could start.
what it means: a week of being filled, at the threshold, before the work begins.
what a scholar hears: milu'im echoes the idiom mille yad, to fill the hand, meaning to ordain; Yoma 2a derives the high priest's seven days of separation before Yom Kippur from Leviticus 8:34.

notes: Leviticus 8:33–35 paraphrased (writer not certain of exact JPS 1917 wording).
Milu'im and the idiom 'fill the hand' (e.g., Exodus 28:41) for ordination: confirm.
Yoma 2a: the high priest's seven-day separation before Yom Kippur derived from Leviticus 8:34: confirm.
The description of what happened during the seven days (offerings repeated, eating at the entrance) follows 8:31–35; confirm.

Audit (second sample): removed the sweeping, preachy aside ('wisdom the modern world mostly skips; we start new jobs on Monday and relationships on a whim') and the stock 'fill with patience, with purpose'; added the red heifer priest's seven-day separation (Mishnah Parah 3:1; Yoma 2a). Confirm.
